title: Customer impact tiering and message maps
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose: This page defines a lightweight, repeatable model for mapping technical signals (SLOs, errors, latency, capacity) to customer-impact tiers and prescriptive message maps for status page updates, proactive customer emails, and CS/SE talking points. It is intended for on-call responders, customer success, sales, and communications teams so we deliver consistent, timely, and accurate messages during partial degradations and incidents.

Scope: covers incident classification, message timing and cadence, per-tier templates (status page, email, in-product banner), owner roles, rollback governance, and game-day validation checks. Does not replace specific runbooks for service-specific remediation — link to runbooks for technical steps.

Definitions and decision rules

- Customer-impact tiers (CAT): a short set of discrete impact levels used company-wide. Use the first matching rule in the order shown.

1) CAT-1 (Severe outage)
   - Definition: SLO breaches affecting majority (>50%) of customers or critical API endpoints returning >=50% error rate or regional outage causing global routing failure.
   - Example signals: >50% 5xx on inference API across region for 5+ minutes, control plane unavailability.
   - Business effect: Product unusable for primary workflows, immediate revenue/SLAs impacted.

2) CAT-2 (Partial outage / significant degradation)
   - Definition: High error rates or latency impacting multiple customers or a single large customer; degradation of non-critical features that materially hinder workflows.
   - Example signals: 10–50% error rate on a commonly used endpoint, median latency >3x baseline for 10+ minutes.
   - Business effect: Noticeable impact; some retries or fallback reduce full outage risk.

3) CAT-3 (Minor degradation / intermittent errors)
   - Definition: Small fraction (<10%) of requests affected, increased retries, or elevated error floor that does not meaningfully block customer workflows.
   - Example signals: spike in 429/503 for isolated routes; slight KV cache miss storm.

4) CAT-4 (Informational / scheduled maintenance)
   - Definition: Planned maintenance windows, configuration changes with pre-announced impact, or informational alerts that do not affect functional behavior.

Escalation and ownership matrix

- Initial responder (Pager) responsibilities:
  - Triage and confirm signal accuracy (logs, metrics, traces).
  - Determine CAT level within first 10 minutes.
  - Assign incident owner and stakeholder leads (Engineering lead, CS on-call, Communications).
  - Kick off bridge if CAT-1 or CAT-2.

- Incident owner (Engineering) responsibilities:
  - Lead technical remediation, track timeline, and update incident timeline.
  - Approve final technical description for public comms.

- Customer Success responsibilities:
  - Decide targeted customer outreach (who to email, which accounts to prioritize).
  - Draft proactive customer messages using the message maps below.
  - Maintain the account escalation list and liaise with Sales/AMs for strategic customers.

- Communications responsibilities:
  - Sanity-check wording for public-facing messages and coordinate status page cadence.
  - Publish status updates per cadence below.

Message cadence and publication rules

- CAT-1:
  - Status page: Create initial status incident within 15 minutes. Update every 30 minutes while active (or sooner if material change).
  - Proactive email: Within 30 minutes to affected customers (prioritize largest accounts); include impact summary, mitigations, expected next update window.
  - In-product banner: Show for customers with live traffic to affected region if feasible.

- CAT-2:
  - Status page: Create incident within 30 minutes. Updates every 60 minutes.
  - Proactive email: Within 90 minutes for customers showing error volume or high importance.
  - In-product banner: Optional; evaluated by CS lead.

- CAT-3:
  - Status page: Optional informational entry after incident if persistent beyond 2 hours.
  - Proactive email: Rare — only for customers with direct impact or contractual obligations.

- CAT-4:
  - Status page: Publish scheduled maintenance notice at least 48 hours in advance.
  - Proactive email: As part of normal maintenance communications.

Message maps (templates)

Each template includes: 1) headline, 2) one-sentence summary, 3) impact details, 4) current mitigation/remediation actions, 5) customer guidance, 6) next update ETA, 7) link to status page. Replace bracketed text.

- CAT-1 status page template (urgent)
  - Headline: Major service disruption affecting [service/region]
  - Summary: We are investigating an ongoing disruption affecting [brief scope — e.g., inference API in us-west-2].
  - Impact: Customers may experience failed requests and timeouts for [affected endpoints].
  - Action: Our engineering team has a high-priority incident open and is actively working on mitigating the root cause.
  - Guidance: Retry logic is recommended; we will provide recommended backoff values in the next update.
  - ETA: Next update in 30 minutes.
  - Link: [Status page URL]

- CAT-1 proactive email template (high-priority customers)
  - Subject: Urgent: Disruption to [service/region] — immediate actions and status
  - Body: Hello [Name], we are investigating a major disruption affecting [scope]. We know this impacts [expected customer impact]. Our engineers are working on a fix. Next update: ~30 minutes. If you need immediate assistance, contact [CS on-call contact].

- CAT-2 status page template (degradation)
  - Headline: Reduced performance for [service/region]
  - Summary: We’re seeing elevated errors/latency that may affect some customers.
  - Impact: [Describe functionality affected].
  - Action: Mitigation in progress (workaround: [e.g., route to fallback model], mitigation ETA: [time]).
  - ETA: Next update in 60 minutes.

- CAT-2 proactive email template
  - Subject: Notice: Degradation affecting [service/region]
  - Body: Hi [Name], we are experiencing degraded performance for [scope]. We have applied [mitigation] and expect improvements within [ETA]. We will follow up with a full incident summary.

- CAT-3 public note (if created)
  - Headline: Intermittent errors observed for [route]
  - Summary: We observed a short-lived spike in error rates; monitoring suggests the issue is isolated and has been mitigated.

Message styling and content constraints

- Tone: factual, concise, non-speculative. Avoid technical jargon when addressing customers, but include technical detail for targeted emails to technical owners.
- Do not assign blame or speculate on root cause. Use language like “investigating,” “mitigating,” and “under active investigation.”
- Include estimated impact and clear next update window. If you don’t have an ETA, state when the next update will be sent rather than promising a timeline.

Status page governance table

| Field | Owner | SLA for first update | Update cadence while active | Visibility |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Initial incident creation | Pager/Responder | 15 minutes (CAT-1), 30 minutes (CAT-2) | n/a | Public |
| Technical details approved | Incident owner | 30 minutes | As needed | Public/internal |
| Business impact summary | CS lead | 30 minutes | 30–60 min | Public |
| Customer-targeted emails | CS lead | 30–90 minutes | As needed | Restricted list |

Runbook quick reference: from signal to customer message (10-minute checklist)

1. Confirm the signal: validate metrics and logs; rule out instrumentation noise.
2. Determine CAT level using definitions above.
3. Assign incident owner and CS lead; create bridge if CAT-1/2.
4. Publish initial status page entry per CAT cadence.
5. Draft proactive email using the appropriate template and prioritize recipients.
6. Post update to internal channel #incident-ops with short summary and link to status page.
7. Track updates in incident timeline and ensure every public update is approved by incident owner and CS lead.

Post-incident requirements

- For CAT-1 and CAT-2 incidents, within 72 hours:
  - Publish a postmortem draft with timeline, root cause hypothesis, mitigation steps, and action items.
  - CS to compile customer impact list and any contractual/regulatory obligations for reporting.
  - Communications to produce a customer-facing summary that is non-technical and approved by Legal if required.

Game day exercises and validation checks

- Frequency: Quarterly regional game days; include at least one cross-functional exercise per quarter that tests message maps and targeted outreach.
- Scenarios to test: partial latency spike, spike in 429s for a top-10 customer, region-level service disruption, and false-positive alert recovery.
- Success criteria: status page entry created within target SLA, initial customer email sent on time for simulated affected accounts, and debrief identifies at least one improvement to message map or cadence.

Training and runbook ownership

- Maintain owner list: every service must list a CS owner and an engineering incident owner in its runbook. Owners must review this message map every 6 months.
- On-call coaching: new responders must shadow two incidents and complete a simulated communication exercise before full ownership of CS outbound messages.

Appendix: quick templates (copy / paste)

- Status page minimal JSON payload (for automation)
  - {\n    \"incident\": \"[short headline]\",\n    \"status\": \"investigating/identified/monitoring/resolved\",\n    \"impact\": \"[brief]\",\n    \"updates\": [{\"time\":\"[ISO]\",\"body\":\"[text]\",\"author\":\"[name]\"}]\n    }\n
- Customer email subject line guidelines:
  - Urgent: [service] disruption in [region] — immediate actions
  - Notice: Degraded performance for [service] — temporary mitigation applied

Known gaps / future enhancements

- Automate initial impact detection mapping from signal detectors to suggested CAT level.
- Build account-level router so proactive emails are generated and queued automatically for affected customers.
